items.title: Being apolitical in India is a luxury and an illusion  | LME 171 | Pooja Prasanna
items.summary: How many times have you heard someone say "I don’t get into politics. I just focus on my career" Or when there are protests, you hear people ask, "Why does everything have to be politicized?" It may sound balanced. But let us be honest for a second. In India, being "apolitical" is a luxury. It is also an illusion, and frankly, it is impossible. Every week on Let Me Explain , we break down complex things—a law, a court judgment, or a government policy. But today, I want to make a simple submission. Being apolitical is plain laziness, and complaining about "politicizing" an issue, any issue, is complete hogwash. Let me explain. Sitting on the fence is not neutrality. It is a decision, a choice. You are deciding to back the status quo. Politics is not restricted to Parliament or election rallies. Politics is the price of your groceries. It is the quality of the air in your lungs, the speed of your Wi-Fi, the fairness of your exams, and whether you get home safely at night. items.title: Only Supreme Court can say its judgment will not be cited as precedent: Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently held that only the Supreme Court can give a caveat that its judgment will not be cited as a precedent. A Division Bench of Justices C Hari Shankar and Vinod Kumar said that such a power is not available to any other court. “This caveat is, therefore, unique to the Supreme Court, as its decisions are constitutionally binding by virtue of Article 141 of the Constitution of India,” the Bench explained. It said that even if the facts of a case are similar to those in an earlier Supreme Court judgment, a lower court cannot treat that judgment as binding precedent if the Supreme Court itself has clarified that it should not apply in such circumstances. In such cases, the binding effect of Article 141 of the Constitution would not apply. Further, the Bench reasoned that if other courts say that their judgments will not be cited as a precedent, it could result in a situation in which similarly placed litigants would receive different treatment. “Ex facie, this would be impermissible,” the Court added. items.title: From consumer consent to competition control: The vires of Rule 5(6)
items.summary: The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026, notified on September 9, 2026 under Section 101(2)(zg) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, contain a provision that deserves closer scrutiny than its privacy-facing language suggests. Rule 5(6), which takes effect on January 1, 2027, provides that no marketplace e-commerce entity shall use information collected by it: - first, for the sale of goods, directly or indirectly, by any seller, whether related or not, bearing a brand or name common with that of the marketplace or - second, to promote or advertise any seller as being associated with the marketplace, unless express and affirmative consent for such use has been obtained from the consumer concerned. The provision speaks the language of consent, but the conduct it regulates has an obvious competition dimension as regards a marketplace using what it knows about consumers to advantage a connected seller over others on the same platform. The question this raises is not whether such conduct should be regulated, but whether the Consumer Protection Act authorises the Central government to regulate it through delegated legislation. items.title: Lawyer can't be faulted for asking NCLT to upload its order on website: NCLAT
items.summary: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) recently held that an advocate cannot be faulted for sending an email to the court master of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) requesting that a judicial order passed by NCLT be uploaded on its website [Mrinal Vs Hynite] The order copy had remained unavailable for 18 days after the pronouncement. A bench of Judicial Member Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan and Technical Member Naresh Salecha deleted the adverse remarks made by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) against advocate Mrinal Harsh Vardhan, who had emailed the NCLT court master asking that the order be uploaded. The NCLAT found that the email was polite and merely reflected the advocate's anxiety to obtain the order. " Naturally when the order which was pronounced in the open Court on 05.06.2026 could not be uploaded for 18 days, we do not find any error in the act of the Appellant in sending an e-mail to the Court Master of the concerned Bench, requesting only for the uplodation of the order which was admittedly pronounced in the open Court on 05.06.2026 ," the NCLAT observed. The case arose from insolvency proceedings concerning Hynite Farms Private Limited.
